entry.title: Mazda 3e: Why Mazda Should Take Another Shot at the Small EV
entry.summary: Mazda has already taken one shot at the compact electric car. The MX-30 brought distinctive styling and some genuinely interesting ideas, but its limited electric range and unconventional packaging left it struggling to compete as the EV market rapidly moved forward. That increasingly left Mazda in a difficult position. Its continued reliance…
entry.content:
Mazda has already taken one shot at the compact electric car. The MX-30 brought distinctive styling and some genuinely interesting ideas, but its limited electric range and unconventional packaging left it struggling to compete as the EV market rapidly moved forward.

That increasingly left Mazda in a difficult position. Its continued reliance on petrol engines and limited range of electrified models put growing pressure on the brand as European emissions rules tightened and manufacturers faced increasingly demanding EV sales targets.

But Mazda’s position now looks very different. A new generation of electric models is beginning to arrive, bringing substantially more competitive technology, range and pricing. TNY Design Studio asks whether Mazda should take the next logical step — and bring that new EV formula back down into the heart of the European market.


Mazda’s EV story has changed dramatically over the past year. The 6e marked the first major step, combining long-range electric powertrains and significantly more technology with the traditional proportions of a large, low-slung saloon. Just as importantly, Mazda has managed to price it competitively, giving the brand a far more convincing electric proposition than before.

Now the CX-6e takes that formula into the SUV market. Its exterior feels distinctly Mazda, while inside, the wide digital dashboard and clean layout give it a striking, modern character without losing the sense of quality expected from one of the brand’s larger models.

Together, the 6e and CX-6e represent a considerable reset. The question now is whether Mazda can take the same ingredients and successfully bring them further down the range. (Image credit: Mazda)


The Mazda3 has been one of the most important cars in Mazda’s European range for more than two decades, combining distinctive design and a more upmarket feel with the dimensions and usability expected of a conventional family hatchback. Keeping that position relevant as the market moves towards EVs could increasingly require more than efficient combustion engines and hybrids.

Our Mazda 3e rendering explores one possible answer: effectively bringing the thinking behind the 6e into a smaller, roughly 4.4-metre hatchback. It retains Mazda’s familiar proportions and sporting character, but combines them with the cleaner surfaces and EV-focused details of its newest models.

Done properly, a smaller 6e could give Mazda a credible rival to the growing number of electric hatchbacks now competing at the heart of the European market.


Mazda has already shown that it understands the appeal of a compact SUV. The CX-3 and CX-30 have both given the brand attractive, relatively small family crossovers, but combustion-powered models alone do little to solve the emissions challenge Mazda faces in Europe. With European fleet CO₂ requirements tightening, higher-volume electric models could become particularly valuable to Mazda.

Our CX-3e rendering explores what happens if Mazda applies its new EV formula to this part of the market. Smaller and more affordable than the CX-6e, it could combine the design character of Mazda’s latest SUVs with a fully electric powertrain in one of Europe’s most important segments.

Alongside a 3e hatchback, it could give Mazda two genuinely useful volume EVs rather than relying primarily on larger, more expensive models.


This is not the first time TNY Design Studio has explored what could come next for Mazda. In our earlier look at the brand’s future, we imagined the MX-X — a compact Mazda3-sized saloon with a cleaner, more sporting interpretation of Mazda’s evolving design language.

That rendering was originally imagined with a combustion engine, right down to its twin exhausts, but the basic design could translate particularly well into an EV. Remove those exhausts, optimise the proportions around an electric platform and introduce some of the detailing now seen on the 6e, and the result could offer another direction for a future Mazda3 family.

It also shows that going electric does not have to mean abandoning the simple, elegant shapes that have helped distinguish Mazda from its rivals. (Image credit: TNY Design Studio)


The MX-30 ultimately showed that distinctive design alone was not enough to make a competitive electric Mazda. Limited range, an unconventional body and relatively high pricing restricted its appeal at a time when the wider EV market was moving quickly.
Mazda now has an opportunity to approach the smaller end of the market very differently.

The 6e and CX-6e demonstrate how access to new technology and partnerships can sit alongside recognisable Mazda design, while delivering the range, equipment and value increasingly expected from an EV.

A 3e could bring that formula into the heart of the European hatchback market, while a CX-3e could give Mazda the electric small SUV capable of generating meaningful volume.

Neither exists today, but Mazda has already shown it is prepared to rethink its EV strategy. This time, going smaller could be every bit as important as going further. (Image credit: Mazda)

entry.title: Volvo’s 13-Car Plan — Design Studio Explores the New Range
entry.summary: Volvo has changed dramatically under Geely ownership. What was already a respected premium brand has gained the investment, technology and global scale needed to compete far more directly with the likes of BMW and Mercedes-Benz. That is a significant shift from the Ford era, when Volvo produced some excellent cars but often…
entry.content:
Volvo’s SUV range is already one of the most complete it has ever offered, stretching from the compact EX30 through to the new flagship EX90 and family-friendly XC90. And there is considerably more to come: Volvo recently outlined a 13-model product offensive, with seven new or substantially updated models planned for Europe.

Volvo has not revealed what all of those cars will be, leaving plenty of room for speculation over how broadly its next generation of models could expand.

The EX60 shows just how far EV technology has progressed. Built around the new SPA3 architecture, its 800V electrical system supports rapid charging, while the longest-range P12 version offers up to 503 miles of WLTP range — the longest of any Volvo yet. 

Estates have been central to Volvo’s identity for generations. From the boxy 240 and 740 through the 850 and V70, and later the V60 and V90, Volvo built much of its reputation around cars that combined huge practicality with understated Scandinavian design. Yet as buyers have moved towards SUVs, that once-defining part of the range has steadily diminished.


A “low-roof” SPA3 model would not necessarily have to be an estate. Volvo could also use the architecture for an ES60, giving it a smaller electric saloon beneath the ES90 and a more direct alternative to the next generation of electric BMW 3 Series.

Our rendering imagines exactly that: a lower, sportier Volvo that carries the clean design language of the ES90 into a more compact package. It could give Volvo a genuinely different proposition from the EX60, while filling a sizeable gap between its smaller models and the large ES90.

Volvo has experimented here before, even creating the unusual raised S60 Cross Country in 2015. We wouldn’t expect an ES60 Cross Country revival, but the standard saloon could make considerably more sense as Volvo broadens its electric range.


An estate does not necessarily have to remain low-slung, either. Volvo has been combining estate-car practicality with additional ride height and rugged styling since the original V70 Cross Country arrived in 1997, creating a formula that has since become an important part of the brand.

An EV60 Cross Country could revive that idea for the electric era. Raised suspension, protective bodywork and all-wheel drive could give buyers much of the visual appeal and capability of an SUV, while retaining the lower roofline, efficiency and long load area of an estate. It could also help Volvo justify an electric estate commercially by broadening its potential audience.

Yet Volvo's ambitions may not stop at reviving traditional strengths. Its new-generation technology also gives the brand the flexibility to explore territory beyond its current flagship models.

This is where Volvo’s plans become particularly interesting. SPA3 has been designed to scale far beyond the EX60, with Volvo previously saying it could support cars both smaller than the EX30 and larger than the EX90. That gives Volvo the technical flexibility to enter territory it does not currently occupy, should it see a commercial case for doing so.

Our ES100 rendering explores what that upper extreme could look like: a large, luxurious electric saloon positioned against cars such as the BMW i7 and Mercedes EQS, with Scandinavian design offering a deliberately different take on the traditional flagship.


The same thinking could also produce a larger SUV. Our EX100 rendering imagines Volvo stretching the formula beyond the EX90, creating something longer, more spacious and considerably more luxurious — a Scandinavian alternative to the Mercedes GLS.

Rather than simply making another three-row family SUV, the emphasis could shift towards outright luxury. A longer wheelbase could provide significantly more space for second- and third-row passengers, while Volvo’s latest EV technology, minimalist interiors and emphasis on comfort would suit this end of the market particularly well.

It would be a considerable step upwards for Volvo, but if the flexibility is already being engineered into its next-generation architecture, an EX100 provides an interesting glimpse at how the brand could use it.


Ultimately, the most interesting part of Volvo’s 13-car product offensive may not be the possibility of enormous new flagships at all. The ES100 and EX100 show how far Volvo could theoretically stretch its new technology, but the greater opportunity could be using that flexibility to broaden the range closer to its existing core.

SUVs will undoubtedly remain central to Volvo’s future, and models such as the EX30, EX60 and EX90 give it a strong foundation. But that does not mean every new Volvo needs to follow the same formula.

An ES60 could restore a smaller premium saloon, while an EV60 could bring the electric estate into one of the segments where Volvo has historically been strongest. Add an EV60 Cross Country, and Volvo could even bridge the gap between its estate heritage and today’s appetite for SUVs.

For a brand entering another period of expansion, becoming broader again could be just as important as becoming bigger.

entry.title: Audi’s Next Chapter: A2, E5 and a New Push Upmarket
entry.summary: Audi wants to move upmarket, but its product strategy is starting to pull in two very different directions. In China, the new E5 Sportback shows just how far the brand can go, combining 800V charging, advanced software and a new generation of digital architecture developed with SAIC. In Europe, meanwhile, Audi is…
entry.content:
The E5 shows just how much Audi and SAIC have already achieved together. For roughly £30,000 in China — around half the price of a comparable A6 e-tron in Britain — it can combine an 800V architecture with a battery of up to 100kWh, as much as 787PS and charging approaching 400kW, enough to add around 370km of range in just ten minutes.

The long-range A6 e-tron also uses a 100kWh battery and 800V architecture, yet charging peaks at 270kW. The E5 is therefore not simply a cheaper Audi developed for China; in some important technical areas, it is already ahead of Audi’s European range. If Audi genuinely wants to move further upmarket, SAIC could help bring that faster development and more advanced EV technology west.

It is particularly telling that the E5 not only charges faster than Audi’s halo e-tron GT, but also brings a more advanced software architecture. And that technology is not entirely confined to China: SAIC already offers similar hardware in Britain through the MG IM5 and IM6, with 800V systems and 100kWh versions capable of charging from 10–80% in around 17 minutes. The IM5 Long Range also reaches up to 441 miles WLTP. (Image Credit: Audi)

The A2 e-tron is, on paper, an impressive small EV. Audi quotes up to 397 miles under WLTP testing, while extensive aerodynamic optimisation, including active cooling, a smoother underbody and dedicated aero wheels, helps it pull ahead of its ID.3 and Cupra Born siblings.

The problem is strategic. Does Audi, while talking about moving further upmarket, really need another £30,000-something hatchback sharing its foundations with its Volkswagen Group siblings?

You could almost argue that the A2 makes more sense as the electric car that could have saved SEAT. If Volkswagen Group genuinely believed there was still room for a value-focused mainstream brand, a practical, efficient and relatively affordable EV like this feels closer to SEAT's historical role than Audi's future ambitions.

The A2 therefore enters one of the most fiercely contested parts of the EV market. Beyond Volkswagen Group, increasingly capable rivals from Kia, MG, Leapmotor and Tesla are putting pressure on both price and specification. With the Tesla Model 3 now starting below £38,000 in Britain, there is only so far a premium-badged compact EV can stretch its value proposition.

The A7 Sportback could be where those ambitions start to make the most sense. A long, low electric fastback would give the brand a more natural way to chase BMW and Mercedes, while also opening the door to the sort of sleek aerodynamics needed to join the 500-mile EV range club. The E5’s electrical and software architecture could form the basis of a more convincing European flagship.
With the A7 already gone and the current A8 now at the end of its production run, Audi has effectively vacated the traditional flagship saloon space just as BMW and Mercedes continue to invest heavily in the i7 and EQS. A new A8 could restore that clear halo role, giving the brand somewhere to showcase its best charging, software, suspension and cabin technology.

Without direct electric rivals to the BMW i7 and Mercedes-Benz EQS, Audi risks ceding the luxury EV flagship segment to its competitors and competing from the middle of the premium market instead.
A new flagship architecture would not have to serve Audi alone. It could also support other premium Volkswagen Group brands. Bentley’s Flying Spur remains a plug-in hybrid, while the newly revealed Torcal SUV is its first fully electric production model.

A suitably flexible A8 architecture could potentially underpin a future electric Bentley saloon too — keeping Crewe’s range from becoming overly SUV-focused while spreading the cost of another high-end electric platform across two premium brands.


The Q8 gives Audi another route upmarket without abandoning the SUV buyers that now dominate the premium market. Positioned as the sportier, more design-led counterpart to the Q7 and beneath the larger Q9, it can act as Audi’s halo performance SUV rather than another family-focused seven-seater.

Importantly, the Q8’s future has recently been secured. Audi CEO Gernot Döllner revealed that when he joined Audi there was no decision to replace it, but that the company has since reversed course and approved a next-generation Q8.

Our rendering imagines that successor using Audi’s new design language, while keeping the lower, more dramatic stance that gives the Q8 a distinct role alongside the Q7 and Q9.


Audi’s challenge now is not a lack of technology, but deciding where that technology should take the brand next. The A2 e-tron may be a strong small EV, yet the bigger opportunity arguably lies further up the range, where Audi can create more space between itself and its Volkswagen Group relatives while better justifying premium pricing.

The E5 has already shown what Audi and SAIC can achieve together. And with SAIC already bringing similar technology to Britain through MG, the question becomes harder to ignore: why couldn’t more of it find its way into Audi’s European range?

If Audi can bring those lessons into a new generation of A7, A8 and Q8 models, it may finally have the foundations for a more clearly defined and genuinely more upmarket future. (Image Credit: TNY Design Studio)

entry.title: Lucid’s UK Push – Cosmos, Earth and a Much Bigger Plan
entry.summary: Lucid is in an unusual position. The American EV maker regularly attracts headlines about losses, cash burn and funding requirements, yet at the same time it is expanding its manufacturing footprint, attracting major strategic partners and preparing an entirely new lower-cost vehicle family for markets including Britain. Its current cars already demonstrate…
entry.content:
Lucid is in an unusual position. The American EV maker regularly attracts headlines about losses, cash burn and funding requirements, yet at the same time it is expanding its manufacturing footprint, attracting major strategic partners and preparing an entirely new lower-cost vehicle family for markets including Britain.

Its current cars already demonstrate just how far Lucid’s engineering can go. The Air Sapphire produces 1,234hp, reaches 60mph in 1.89 seconds and tops out at 205mph, while the opposite end of the Air’s talents is demonstrated by the Grand Touring, which offers up to 512 miles of EPA range — or around 597 miles under WLTP testing.


The Cosmos will be the first Lucid developed from the outset with right-hand-drive markets in mind, making it the model expected to finally bring the brand to Britain in 2027. Patent images and development cars have already revealed much of its sleek, cab-forward shape.

Underneath sits Lucid’s new Midsize architecture, using an 800V electrical system and the smaller, cheaper Atlas drive unit. Lucid says the platform will start below $50,000; for Britain, we think around £45,000 is a realistic starting point.

Exact dimensions remain unconfirmed, but its Model Y/EX60 positioning suggests something around 4.7–4.8 metres long, with a long wheelbase prioritising cabin space.


Battery chemistry is another unanswered question. Lucid has not confirmed LFP for Cosmos, although it would be a logical way of controlling entry-model costs; equally, Lucid’s strategy is explicitly based on achieving competitive range with a smaller battery, rather than simply fitting ever larger packs.

We would not expect it to chase the £37,990 Tesla Model 3 on price — Tesla should remain one of Europe’s strongest range-per-pound propositions. Instead, Cosmos looks set to occupy a more premium space: think £42,990 Mazda CX-6e at one end and the £56,860 Volvo EX60 above it, combining a plush cabin with sophisticated EV architecture and Lucid’s particular obsession with efficiency.


Earth takes the Midsize formula in a more practical direction. Lucid describes it as the more adventurous sibling to Cosmos, and the official covered silhouette suggests a squarer roofline and more upright rear — exactly the sort of family SUV Lucid will need if it wants meaningful volume in the premium midsize market.

Our Design Studio interpretation therefore keeps the same clean Lucid face and low bonnet, but gives Earth a more substantial body and greater emphasis on passenger and luggage space. Underneath, it should share the new Midsize architecture and Atlas drive technology with Cosmos.

For a brand currently best known for expensive Air and Gravity models, Earth could ultimately be the more important product: a direct route into the heart of the premium SUV market.

Lucid also enters this expansion with backing few EV start-ups can match. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund has supported the company since 2018 and remains its majority shareholder. Lucid's financial backing also continued to grow in 2026. PIF affiliate Ayar committed a further $550 million, Uber increased its investment by $200 million to $500 million in total, and Lucid raised another $300 million through a share offering.


The Air Sapphire shows what Lucid has already learned to do at the very top of the market. Beyond its extreme performance, the Air combines a spacious five-metre luxury-car package with sophisticated software, high-end materials, advanced driver-assistance technology and an exceptionally aerodynamic body despite its striking design.

Gravity has since taken many of those ideas into a large SUV. The challenge now is to bring that same engineering philosophy down into cars costing far less.

Cosmos, Earth and the wider Midsize family will use simpler, lower-cost hardware such as the Atlas drive unit, smaller batteries and greater component sharing, but Lucid is clearly trying to preserve the things that made Air distinctive: efficiency, range, interior quality and genuinely advanced EV architecture. Image Credit: Lucid Motors


The next step takes Lucid beyond conventional private cars. On 17 September 2026, Lucid and European mobility company Bolt announced plans to co-develop an autonomous vehicle around the new Midsize platform.

The announcement did not disclose an investment figure or describe Bolt as taking an equity stake in Lucid, but Bolt intends to own and operate at least 25,000 vehicles across European cities.

Our Design Studio interpretation imagines what that could mean: a shorter bonnet, long four-seat passenger compartment, no steering wheel and autonomous hardware integrated from the outset, rather than added later. It keeps the clean Lucid lighting and aerodynamic surfacing, but puts passenger space and easy urban use ahead of the more sporting proportions of Cosmos.


This is not simply another Waymo-style conversion of an existing production car. Lucid and Bolt say they will develop an ADS-ready vehicle from the product-development stage, using NVIDIA’s Hyperion architecture and targeting SAE Level 4 autonomy.

Bolt’s initial 25,000-car commitment forms part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform by 2035, with the Lucids expected to be produced at the company’s expanding Saudi Arabian facility.

That potentially puts the project somewhere between Waymo’s sensor-equipped Jaguar I-Pace approach and Tesla’s purpose-built two-seat Cybercab: still recognisably a car, but designed around autonomous ride-hailing from the beginning. Image Credit: Lucid Motors


Lucid’s challenge is no longer proving that it can build an impressive electric car. Air and Gravity have already done that. The next phase is about scale: taking the efficiency, performance, software and premium feel of those expensive models and making them work in products that can attract far more buyers.

Cosmos and Earth are the key to that transition, while the autonomous programme shows Lucid’s technology could also become valuable well beyond private ownership.

There are still big questions around profitability, pricing and how quickly production can ramp, but Lucid now has something many young EV brands never achieve: a recognisable design language, class-leading efficiency and highly advanced EV engineering, major financial backing and several credible routes to growth.

If the Midsize family lands at the right price, Britain could be seeing Lucid at exactly the point it starts becoming much harder to ignore.

Images: TNY Design Studio renderings are speculative interpretations based on available information at the time of publication. The comparison table combines TNY Design Studio renderings with official Lucid Motors imagery. Data: Prices are approximate US starting prices, rounded to the nearest $5,000 where stated. Estimated future-model figures are marked “est.” Specifications, range and performance figures were correct to the best of our knowledge at the time of publication and may change before production.

entry.title: MAXUS Pre-Reg Watch: Five Big Discounts Worth Knowing About
entry.summary: MAXUS has become one of the more interesting value brands in the UK commercial vehicle market, with a range that now stretches from diesel and electric vans to pickups and large MPVs. Backed by SAIC Motor, it has steadily built its case around equipment, electrification and aggressive pricing. That value argument becomes…
entry.content:
MAXUS T60 MAX
RRP: £41,994 incl. VAT
Pre-reg: £29,994 incl. VAT
Saving: £12,000 — 28.6%


MAXUS eTERRON 9
RRP: £63,600 incl. VAT
Pre-reg: £47,994 incl. VAT
Saving: £15,606 — 24.5%

MAXUS MIFA 7
RRP: £49,560 incl. VAT
Pre-reg: £36,000 incl. VAT
Saving: £13,560 — 27.4%


MAXUS eDELIVER 7
RRP: £46,435 + VAT
Pre-reg: £19,496 + VAT
Saving: £26,939 + VAT — 58.0%

MAXUS DELIVER 9
RRP: £32,493 + VAT
Pre-reg: £19,296 + VAT
Saving: £13,197 + VAT — 40.6%

The DELIVER 9 is no longer an unfamiliar Chinese newcomer. It has been on UK roads since 2020 and, after several years of fleet sales, has become a relatively common sight. This is a full-size large van with up to 12.9m³ of load space, a 2.0-litre diesel engine and a choice of front- or rear-wheel drive, putting it firmly into Transit, Boxer and Movano territory.

At £19,296 + VAT pre-reg, though, it costs considerably less than most equivalent large vans. For buyers who simply need a lot of usable van for their money, the DELIVER 9 makes a particularly strong value case.

Taken together, these five deals show how aggressively MAXUS is competing on value. The biggest reductions are on the eDELIVER 7 and DELIVER 9, but even the pickups and MIFA 7 are being advertised well below list price.

MAXUS may still lack the badge recognition of some established rivals, but at these pre-reg prices it becomes much harder to dismiss — particularly for buyers more interested in capability, equipment and usable range than the name on the grille.

Prices and specifications were correct at the time of publication and may change without notice. Pre-registered prices are based on advertised UK stock and may vary by dealer, specification and availability. RRP figures refer to official UK list prices; commercial vehicle prices are shown excluding VAT where stated. Images courtesy of MAXUS/SAIC Motor.

entry.title: Peugeot 6008: The Flagship SUV Nobody Expected
entry.summary: Stellantis’ Chinese story is increasingly dominated by Leapmotor, but another partnership is quietly becoming important again. Dongfeng has worked with Peugeot and Citroën in China for more than three decades, yet that relationship is often overlooked in today’s Stellantis narrative. Now that partnership has produced two particularly significant Peugeot concepts. Concept 6…
entry.content:
Stellantis’ Chinese story is increasingly dominated by Leapmotor, but another partnership is quietly becoming important again. Dongfeng has worked with Peugeot and Citroën in China for more than three decades, yet that relationship is often overlooked in today’s Stellantis narrative.

Now that partnership has produced two particularly significant Peugeot concepts. Concept 6 previews a sleek, low-slung large car, while Concept 8 points towards a new flagship SUV developed through the Dongfeng-Peugeot partnership. Both are being developed towards production models expected to be built in China from 2027.

Concept 8 may soon become more relevant to Europe. Peugeot had previously indicated that neither Concept 6 nor Concept 8 was intended for the European market, making the latest development particularly curious. French Peugeot specialist Forum-Peugeot now reports that Concept 8 will be brought to France for October’s Paris Motor Show, citing a reliable source.

Concept 8 is intended to be a genuine halo model: a large electric flagship sitting above the 5008, with a production version expected to offer up to seven seats. Peugeot has not released its final dimensions, but its scale puts it much closer in concept to cars such as the Kia EV9 and Hyundai Ioniq 9 than to another conventional family SUV.

That leaves plenty of room above the existing 5008. At 4,791mm long, Peugeot’s current seven-seater is already slightly larger than a Chery Tiggo 8 and Skoda Kodiaq, yet starts at around £37,000 as a hybrid and £39,000 as an E-5008. A larger electric flagship beginning at roughly £60,000 could therefore sit comfortably above it while still undercutting the £65,000-plus EV9 and Ioniq 9.

Concepts 6 and 8 are already being developed towards production in China, with selected export markets also expected to receive the resulting models. Concept 8 is now reported to be heading for the Paris Motor Show, but there has been no equivalent announcement for Concept 6 — which is perhaps a pity.

The sleek fastback reads almost like a natural successor to the 508, Peugeot's previous halo model, which disappeared without a direct replacement as the brand increasingly centred its European range around the slightly smaller 408 crossover and its existing line of SUVs. Image: Peugeot

Peugeot also has good reason to test how far customers are prepared to follow it upmarket. Despite offering the 3008 and 5008 at considerably lower entry prices, British buyers have shown a strong appetite for higher specifications.

During the E-3008's first months on sale, 85% of UK customers chose the range-topping GT trim, compared with 60% across markets. Peugeot has since gone further, introducing an even richer GT Premium specification for both the 3008 and 5008.

Inside, our E-6008 interpretation moves Peugeot's i-Cockpit another step forward, building on the already high-quality cabin design of the current 3008 and 5008. Rather than reinventing it completely, we have imagined how that architecture could evolve for a more expensive flagship — including Peugeot's new Hypersquare steering control.

Hypersquare replaces the conventional steering wheel with a compact rectangular steer-by-wire controller, with no mechanical connection to the front wheels. It varies its response with speed and requires just 170 degrees of rotation in either direction at low speeds. Peugeot plans to introduce the technology on a production model from 2027.

It also feels particularly well suited to Peugeot. The existing i-Cockpit has already spent years positioning a small steering wheel beneath a high-mounted instrument display, so Hypersquare develops an established Peugeot idea rather than introducing an entirely unfamiliar driving position.

Visitors to the 2026 Paris Motor Show are expected to see Concept 8 alongside Peugeot's latest Hypersquare technology, with Peugeot also bringing the Polygon Concept that has acted as a rolling test bed for the technology. Polygon previews the next generation of Peugeot design and technology expected to feed into future models, including the next-generation 208.

That makes Hypersquare a particularly appropriate addition to our imagined E-6008: by the time a production Concept 8 derivative reaches showrooms, this radical-looking control could already be established Peugeot technology. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio — speculative Peugeot E-6008 interior rendering.

From the rear, Concept 8's potential as a Peugeot flagship becomes particularly clear. It is a striking design, but not one that feels completely detached from the brand's current direction. More importantly, there appears to be a plausible European market for it. Peugeot's own customers have already shown a willingness to move towards the more expensive end of its existing range.

That makes next month's Paris Motor Show particularly interesting. Peugeot will put considerable emphasis on its future design and technology, including Hypersquare and the Polygon Concept, as Stellantis uses the show to present a much broader vision of where its brands are heading.

For TNY, two questions stand out. Will Hypersquare become a defining feature that spreads across several Peugeot models, rather than simply appearing on one new generation of car? And, perhaps more importantly, why is Concept 8 reportedly being brought to Paris?

If it were simply a China-focused design exercise, its appearance at Peugeot's home motor show would be less significant. Instead, Paris gives Peugeot an opportunity to put the car directly in front of European customers and gauge the reaction to something considerably larger and more expensive than today's 5008.

We don't yet know whether that will ultimately result in an E-6008 — or whether Europe will receive Concept 8's production descendant at all. But the ingredients are increasingly plausible. If Peugeot wants a flagship again, Concept 8 could provide it with a very different successor to the role once occupied by the 508. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio — speculative Peugeot E-6008 rendering.

entry.title: Nissan Pixo: Could Britain's Former Cheapest Car Make an Electric Comeback?
entry.summary: When the Nissan Pixo arrived in the UK in 2009, it quickly established itself at the very bottom of Britain's new-car market. For the majority of its short life, it was Britain's cheapest new car — a position that became an important part of the little Nissan's identity. Then, in 2013, Dacia…
entry.content:
When the Nissan Pixo arrived in the UK in 2009, it quickly established itself at the very bottom of Britain's new-car market. For the majority of its short life, it was Britain's cheapest new car — a position that became an important part of the little Nissan's identity.

Then, in 2013, Dacia changed the game. The considerably larger Sandero arrived with its now-famous £5,995 starting price, bringing the Pixo's time at the bottom of the market to an abrupt end and resetting expectations of just how much car Britain's cheapest models could offer.

Today, Dacia is once again responsible for Britain's cheapest new car with the Spring. This time, however, a reborn Pixo wouldn't necessarily be fighting Dacia's approach to cheap motoring from the outside. By using the small-EV programme underpinning the new Renault Twingo E-Tech and upcoming Dacia Spring, Nissan could create a genuinely low-cost electric car of its own, sitting substantially below the current Micra EV.

It would return the Pixo to exactly the part of the market where people remember it: simple, small and among the cheapest new cars in Britain. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio

The original Pixo was already a product of collaboration. Rather than developing an ultra-low-cost city car from scratch, Nissan turned to Suzuki, with the Pixo closely related to the contemporary Alto and both cars produced by Maruti Suzuki in India.

That makes the idea of a Renault-developed successor rather more appropriate than it might initially appear. The badge, partner and technology would change, but the philosophy would be remarkably similar: take an existing small-car programme, give it a Nissan identity and use the economies of scale to put Nissan back at the cheapest end of the market.

Nearly two decades later, globalisation has only made that approach more common. Nissan already shares technology extensively with Renault, while the next Twingo and upcoming Dacia Spring provide something its own European range currently lacks — the foundations for a genuinely inexpensive A-segment EV. Image: Nissan

There is something remarkably familiar about three manufacturers sharing the cost of creating a new generation of affordable city cars.

Twenty years ago, Toyota joined forces with Peugeot and Citroën to create the Aygo, 107 and C1. One Japanese manufacturer and two European brands shared the basic engineering and production of three closely related cars, helping make them cheap to buy, cheap to run and viable to produce.

Two decades later, the same Japanese-European formula could be coming back in electric form. This time it is Nissan representing Japan, alongside European partners Renault and Dacia. The new Twingo and upcoming Spring already share their small-EV foundations, while Nissan's upcoming entry-level EV is clearly heading in the same direction, with Twingo-like proportions and a remarkably similar window line.

If that Nissan becomes the Pixo, the parallels will be difficult to miss. Once again, two European brands and one Japanese manufacturer would be sharing the expensive foundations of three distinct city cars, spreading development costs while giving each its own design and identity.


For a while, Europe's city-car segment looked close to extinction. Tiny petrol cars offered manufacturers slim profit margins, while increasingly expensive emissions and safety requirements made developing a new generation difficult to justify. Now electrification and shared platforms are giving the class another chance.

Toyota's Aygo X has gone hybrid, the Fiat 500e has been joined by a new 500 Hybrid, while the Leapmotor T03, Hyundai Inster and Dacia Spring have already pushed small EVs towards genuinely affordable territory.

Next come the new Renault Twingo E-Tech and upcoming Spring, followed by small Hyundai and Kia EVs and Volkswagen Group's new entry-level Volkswagen and Škoda models. Suddenly, Britain could have a surprisingly crowded selection of city cars competing around or below £20,000.

A new Pixo could give Nissan something its emerging electric range currently lacks: a genuinely low-cost entry point. Sitting comfortably below £20,000, it could focus on compact dimensions, simplicity and everyday urban use, leaving the new Micra EV as the more substantial and desirable supermini.

The Leaf then gives Nissan another fresh electric option for buyers wanting something different again, with greater range and a more crossover-like approach. Together, Pixo, Micra and Leaf could give Nissan three distinct new EVs covering different prices and priorities at the smaller end of the market.

A new Pixo wouldn't need to reinvent Nissan's smallest car. In many ways, the strongest argument for bringing the name back is that it could follow exactly the same philosophy as the original: borrow the expensive foundations from elsewhere, add enough Nissan identity to make the result distinctive, and concentrate on keeping the price low.

With the Micra and Leaf already giving Nissan two fresh electric models further up the range, a Pixo priced comfortably below them could complete one of the most convincing small-EV line-ups on the UK market.

The technology would be completely different from 2009, but the objective would be remarkably familiar. If Nissan really wants to put an electric car back near the bottom of Britain's price lists, the Pixo might be exactly the right name for it. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio.

entry.title: Two Cylinders Were Once Enough: The Rise and Fall of the Two-Cylinder Car
entry.summary: For much of the car's history, two cylinders were enough. Small, light and relatively simple, twin-cylinder engines powered everything from basic family transport to some of the world's most distinctive small cars. The Citroën 2CV, Fiat 500 and Subaru 360 helped mobilise millions, while later examples showed just how far the idea…
entry.content:
Morgan Three Wheeler

Citroën 2CV

Few cars are more closely associated with two cylinders than the Citroën 2CV. Launched in 1948, it was designed as simple, inexpensive transport for rural France, combining an air-cooled flat-twin engine with exceptionally soft suspension and a lightweight body. Early cars produced just 9 hp from 375cc, but the engine gradually grew in capacity and power, eventually reaching 602cc in later versions.


Fiat 500

Launched in 1957, the Fiat Nuova 500 approached affordable motoring from a very different direction to the 2CV. At barely three metres long, it was designed to squeeze families and everyday transport into the crowded streets of post-war Italy.

Behind the rear seats sat a tiny air-cooled two-cylinder engine. The original 479cc unit produced just 13 hp, but low weight and extraordinary simplicity made outright power far less important. Later versions gained larger and more powerful engines while retaining the basic twin-cylinder layout.


Subaru 360

Launched in 1958, the Subaru 360 brought the two-cylinder formula to Japan's rapidly developing car market. Built to comply with Japan's kei-car regulations, it measured less than three metres long yet was designed to accommodate four adults — an impressive piece of packaging for the period.

Its rear-mounted 356cc two-cylinder, two-stroke engine kept the mechanical package compact, while lightweight monocoque construction drew on Subaru's aircraft-engineering heritage. Its rounded shape also earned it the affectionate Japanese nickname “Ladybug.”


Fiat 126

Launched in 1972 as the successor to the 500, the Fiat 126 carried the company's two-cylinder formula into a new generation. Its squarer body looked considerably more modern, but underneath remained the familiar rear-engined, air-cooled twin-cylinder layout that had helped make its predecessor so accessible.

Early cars used a 594cc engine, later growing to 652cc, while Polish production transformed the 126 into an important people's car in its own right. More than 3.3 million were eventually produced in Poland, where it became affectionately known as the Maluch, or “little one.”

Remarkably, production continued until 2000. The 126 therefore kept the traditional two-cylinder people's car alive a full decade after the Citroën 2CV had disappeared. Image: Tony Harrison / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)


Citroën Visa

By the time the Citroën Visa arrived in 1978, the company's air-cooled flat-twin had already powered generations of affordable cars. Alongside the 2CV, variants of the engine had appeared in the Ami and Dyane, making two cylinders a familiar part of Citroën's identity.

The Visa was a much more modern proposition, sharing its basic platform with the Peugeot 104. Entry-level Spécial and Club versions nevertheless retained a 652cc evolution of Citroën's flat-twin, while more powerful Visas adopted four-cylinder engines.

It proved to be one of the twin's final appearances in a new Citroën design. The two-cylinder Visa disappeared during the 1980s, remarkably leaving the much older 2CV to carry the flat-twin into 1990 — more than four decades after its introduction. Image: Citroën / Stellantis


Tata Nano

When the Tata Nano reached production in 2009, two cylinders returned for a purpose that would have been familiar decades earlier: making car ownership more accessible. Developed for India, the Nano was conceived as an affordable alternative for families relying on motorcycles and scooters.

Its rear-mounted 624cc petrol engine produced around 35 bhp, driving through a four-speed manual gearbox. Combined with a lightweight body and tiny dimensions, the simple two-cylinder layout helped Tata keep manufacturing costs, weight and fuel consumption down.

The Nano never achieved the huge sales originally envisaged, and production ended in 2018. Nevertheless, it remains a fascinating modern echo of earlier people's cars: a genuinely new vehicle using two cylinders primarily because simplicity and affordability still mattered. Image: Tata Nano — High Contrast / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0 DE)


Fiat 500 TwinAir

In 2010, Fiat returned the two-cylinder engine to mainstream European motoring with the 500 TwinAir. Rather than chasing absolute simplicity, this time the idea was downsizing: using turbocharging and modern engine management to extract useful performance from a tiny engine.

The 875cc turbocharged TwinAir initially produced 85 hp, but Fiat later pushed the tiny engine to 105 hp in the 500. That was remarkable output from just two cylinders, while its distinctive offbeat soundtrack became part of the appeal. Fiat promoted strong official economy and CO₂ figures as major advantages of the compact design.

TwinAir later appeared in several Fiat Group models, but the 500 was its natural home. It demonstrated how sophisticated the two-cylinder engine had become, although real-world economy could fall short of the remarkable official figures. Image: FIAT / Stellantis


Alfa Romeo MiTo TwinAir

If the Fiat 500 was a natural home for the TwinAir engine, the Alfa Romeo MiTo pushed the two-cylinder idea into relatively upmarket territory. Introduced to the UK in 2012, it combined Alfa styling and premium-supermini ambitions with Fiat Group's tiny 875cc turbocharged twin.

What made the MiTo interesting was the contrast. Two-cylinder engines had traditionally belonged to basic cars built around low cost, yet here one appeared in an Alfa Romeo competing with increasingly sophisticated European superminis. Buyers could specify leather, upgraded technology and distinctive styling around one of the smallest engines available.


BMW i3 REx

The BMW i3 took the two-cylinder engine somewhere entirely new. Launched in 2013, the innovative electric hatchback could be ordered as a Range Extender, adding a compact 647cc two-cylinder petrol engine derived from BMW's C 650 GT maxi-scooter.

Unlike a conventional hybrid, the engine never drove the wheels. Instead, it acted as a generator, producing electricity when the battery became depleted. This allowed BMW to extend the i3's usable range while retaining electric propulsion, easing range anxiety when public charging infrastructure was still developing.


Suzuki Celerio

In 2015, Suzuki found another reason for using just two cylinders: extreme diesel efficiency. Developed specifically for India, the Celerio DDiS 125 used Suzuki's first internally developed diesel engine, a tiny 793cc two-cylinder turbo producing 47 hp and 125 Nm.

Performance was modest, but economy was extraordinary. Maruti Suzuki quoted 27.62 km/l, equivalent to roughly 78 mpg (UK), making it India's most fuel-efficient production car at launch. The all-aluminium engine and lightweight Celerio showed how far downsized diesel engineering could be pushed.

The experiment proved short-lived as small diesels increasingly fell from favour. Nevertheless, the Celerio remains one of the strangest final chapters in two-cylinder history: a conventional five-door hatchback powered by an exceptionally small turbodiesel. Image: Maruti Suzuki India / Suzuki


Morgan 3 Wheeler

More than a century after H.F.S. Morgan built his first three-wheeler, the company returned to the same basic idea in 2011. The modern Morgan 3 Wheeler placed a large S&S V-twin prominently ahead of the front axle, immediately recalling the machines that had established Morgan's reputation.

This time, however, two cylinders had little to do with making transport affordable. The exposed engine was deliberately theatrical, contributing vibration, noise and mechanical character to a car designed primarily to make ordinary journeys feel special. Its unusual layout became central to the experience.

Production ended in 2021, and its successor, the Super 3, adopted a Ford three-cylinder engine. It was a fitting final flourish for the two-cylinder car: returning to its earliest roots purely for enjoyment. Image: Morgan Motor Company

Conclusion

Two-cylinder cars probably aren't coming back. Modern emissions requirements, refinement expectations and electrification leave increasingly little reason to accept their inherent compromises.

Yet their influence is enormous. From inexpensive transport for post-war families to turbocharged Fiats, an electrified BMW and a deliberately eccentric Morgan, two cylinders repeatedly proved capable of far more than their size suggested. Their disappearance closes one of motoring's most distinctive engineering chapters.

Important Information

This article is intended for editorial and historical reference. Dates, production figures, engine specifications and other technical information have been checked against manufacturer, archive and reputable historical sources where reasonably available. Specifications may vary by model year, market and individual version.
